standard_text: The human nervous system: the central and peripheral nervous systems; the structure and function of neurons; synapses; the reflex arc; the structure and functions of the brain; the human eye (accommodation, pupillary reflex, binocular vision) and ear (hearing and balance); disorders of the eye and ear. key_big: A reflex is a fast, automatic response.
key_sub: Receptor → sensory neuron → interneuron → motor neuron → effector.
body_html:
How to think about it

The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord; the peripheral nervous system is the nerves. Neurons carry impulses: sensory neurons from receptors, motor neurons to effectors (muscles and glands). Impulses cross synapses using chemical neurotransmitters. A reflex arc gives a quick response without thinking.

The cerebrum controls thought and voluntary actions, the cerebellum controls balance and coordination, and the medulla oblongata controls breathing and heart rate. In the eye, the lens changes shape to focus (accommodation) and the iris controls the size of the pupil. In the ear, the cochlea detects sound and the semicircular canals detect movement for balance.

Example

Which part of the brain controls balance?

Little brain

Answer: the cerebellum

Example

In bright light, what does the pupil do?

Protect the retina

Answer: it becomes smaller

Common mistakes

  • Thinking reflexes are controlled by the cerebrum.
  • Mixing up sensory and motor neurons.
  • Thinking the lens moves forward and backward to focus.

items.q: Is raising your hand to answer a question a reflex action or a voluntary action?
items.e: Reflexes are rapid, automatic and do not need conscious thought; voluntary actions are controlled by the brain consciously.

items.q: Which function is controlled by the medulla oblongata?

items.q: Compare nervous and hormonal control. For hormonal control, what is the area affected?

How is the resting potential kept?
c: the Na⁺/K⁺ pump moves 3 Na⁺ out for every 2 K⁺ in, and K⁺ diffuses out
items.e: The pump uses ATP.

items.q: What is a generator potential?
c: a depolarisation of a receptor membrane caused by a stimulus
items.e: If it reaches threshold, an action potential follows.

items.q: An impulse travels 30 mm along an axon in 0,50 ms. Calculate its speed in m s⁻¹.
Why do myelinated neurones conduct impulses faster?
c: the impulse jumps between nodes of Ranvier (saltatory conduction)
items.e: Depolarisation happens only at the nodes.

items.q: What is the all-or-nothing principle?
c: every stimulus gives an action potential
bigger stimuli give bigger action potentials
action potentials fade along the axon
a stimulus above the threshold always gives a full-size action potential
items.e: Stronger stimuli give more frequent impulses.

items.q: What do Ca²⁺ ions do in muscle contraction?
c: move tropomyosin away from the binding sites on actin
items.e: Released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

items.q: Why do rod cells give higher sensitivity in dim light?
c: each rod has its own neurone
several rods connect to one bipolar neurone (summation)
items.e: Cones give higher visual acuity.

items.q: What does acetylcholinesterase do?
c: breaks down acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft
items.e: This stops continuous stimulation.

items.q: What is the role of the refractory period?
c: it makes impulses travel in one direction and limits their frequency
items.e: Na⁺ channels cannot reopen straight away.

items.q: What causes depolarisation in an action potential?
c: voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open and Na⁺ ions diffuse in
K⁺ channels open and K⁺ leaves
items.e: The inside becomes positive.

items.q: What is the resting potential of a typical neurone?
items.e: The inside is negative compared with the outside.

items.q: Which type of muscle fibre is adapted for endurance?
c: slow-twitch fibres with many mitochondria and myoglobin
items.e: They respire aerobically.

items.q: What causes repolarisation?
c: Na⁺ channels close and voltage-gated K⁺ channels open, so K⁺ diffuses out
items.e: The potential falls back towards rest.

items.q: How does a rise in blood CO₂ change the heart rate?
c: chemoreceptors send more impulses to the medulla, which increases heart rate through sympathetic nerves
items.e: Faster blood flow removes CO₂.

items.q: What is a Pacinian corpuscle?
c: a pressure receptor in the skin
items.e: Pressure deforms stretch-mediated Na⁺ channels.
